props.title: Bad Taste
props.initialSlug: Aliens harvest humans for fast food in gory DIY comedy

sections.content: Peter Jackson's debut feature Bad Taste launched his career with gleefully excessive gore and DIY ingenuity. Shot over four years with friends on weekends, this alien invasion splatter comedy showcases the raw creativity that would later fuel Dead Alive (1992) and The Lord of the Rings (2001-2003). Jackson himself plays two roles, including a hero who literally holds his blown-out brains in place with a belt. The film's handmade practical effects and splatstick humor influenced a generation of guerrilla filmmakers, proving you could make memorable horror with more imagination than money.

sections.content: The late 1980s marked a golden age for horror-comedy, with films pushing practical effects to new extremes. While Re-Animator (1985) and Evil Dead II (1987) had bigger budgets, Bad Taste's no-budget practical effects innovation puts it in league with Street Trash (1987) and Brain Damage (1988) as essential viewing for understanding guerrilla horror filmmaking. These films share a punk rock spirit - treating limited resources as creative fuel rather than limitations.

Jackson's early splatter trilogy (Bad Taste, Meet the Feebles, Dead Alive) demonstrates his evolution as a filmmaker. Each film builds on the previous one's technical ambition while maintaining the same anarchic energy. The practical effects experience gained here directly influenced the groundbreaking work in The Frighteners (1996), which combined practical and early CGI effects in ways that would define Jackson's later blockbuster career. SUBHEAD: The DIY Horror Legacy

movies.title: The Frighteners
movies.slug: Jackson's Hollywood debut follows a psychic con man dealing with a deadly ghost

sections.content: Bad Taste's influence extends beyond just horror-comedy. Its success inspired countless filmmakers to pursue ambitious practical effects on minimal budgets. Slither (2006) director James Gunn has cited it as a major influence, while modern indie horror like Dave Made a Maze (2017) and One Cut of the Dead (2017) carry on its spirit of resourceful filmmaking. The film proves that passionate creators can overcome financial limitations through creativity and determination.
